Decision-maker version
There is no single correct wording. The important test is whether the short version preserves the substantive uncertainty and contextual limits of the full analysis rather than replacing them with a yes/no claim.

2. Leave-one-out

loo <- leave1out(m_primary)
loo

Interpret changes in effect magnitude, intervals and heterogeneity together. Crossing an arbitrary significance threshold is not, by itself, evidence that the scientific conclusion has fundamentally changed.

title: Solution 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
text:
3. Influence diagnostics

inf <- influence(m_primary)
print(inf)
plot(inf)

First check the data and extraction, then understand why the observation is influential: precision, unusual effect size, leverage, or model structure. Exclusion requires a substantive or methodological justification; influence alone is not one.

title: Solution 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
text:
4. Alternative heterogeneity estimator

m_pm <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "PM")

predict(m_primary, transf = exp)
predict(m_pm, transf = exp)

Compare the pooled effect, uncertainty, heterogeneity and prediction interval. The important question is whether the decision-relevant interpretation changes, not whether the estimates are numerically identical.

title: Solution 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
text:
5. Dependence

m_independent <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "REML")

m_multilevel <- rma.mv(
  yi, vi,
  random = ~ 1 | study_id/effect_id,
  data = es,
  method = "REML"
)

The multilevel model better reflects the fact that some effects are nested within the same study. However, as discussed in Module 4, this does not reconstruct unknown sampling covariance caused by shared observations.

title: Solution 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
text:
6. Risk-of-bias sensitivity
A prespecified analysis could compare the primary synthesis of all eligible studies with a model excluding studies judged high risk in the relevant measurement domain. Greater caution would be warranted if excluding those studies materially changed the effect magnitude, uncertainty, prediction interval or direction of the substantive conclusion. The purpose is not to search for a preferred answer but to assess dependence on evidence with a plausible bias mechanism.

title: Solution 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
text:
7. Robustness statement
A strong statement names each tested assumption and describes what changed. For example: results may be stable to the heterogeneity estimator but more sensitive to treatment of dependent effects. The conclusion should therefore be described as robust to the former choice, not as universally “robust”.

title: Solution 4 — Dependence and multilevel meta-analysis
text:
3. Naive model

m_naive <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "REML")
summary(m_naive)

This model treats each row as conditionally independent apart from the common random-effects distribution.

title: Solution 4 — Dependence and multilevel meta-analysis
text:
4. Multilevel model

m_mv <- rma.mv(
  yi = yi,
  V = vi,
  random = ~ 1 | study_id/effect_id,
  data = es,
  method = "REML"
)
summary(m_mv)

The multilevel model partitions heterogeneity at study and effect-within-study levels. With this small synthetic dataset, do not over-interpret numerical differences between models; the exercise is about the changed assumptions.

title: Solution 4 — Dependence and multilevel meta-analysis
text:
5. Variance components

m_mv$sigma2

For ~ 1 | study_id/effect_id, the first component corresponds to study-level heterogeneity and the second to heterogeneity among effects nested within studies. Their substantive meaning depends on what the repeated effects represent.

title: Solution 4 — Dependence and multilevel meta-analysis
text:
6. Limitation
V = vi supplies only diagonal sampling variances. If two effect estimates share a control or repeated observations, their sampling errors can be correlated. Random effects represent heterogeneity in underlying effects; they do not reconstruct an unknown sampling covariance matrix. A full analysis might derive covariance from the study design, assume and vary plausible correlations, aggregate compatible effects, or use suitable cluster-robust inference.

title: Solution 4 — Dependence and multilevel meta-analysis
text:
7. Example interpretation
The dataset contains multiple estimates from some studies, so treating every row as independent can give prolific studies too much information and understate uncertainty. A multilevel model recognises the clustering of effects and separates study-level from within-study heterogeneity. However, the available teaching data do not identify sampling correlations created by shared observations or controls. In a full review we would map those relationships during extraction and assess whether conclusions are robust to defensible covariance or aggregation assumptions.

title: Solution 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
library(metafor)
soil <- read.csv("../data/teaching/soil_carbon.csv")

es <- escalc(
  measure = "ROM",
  m1i = mean_reduced, sd1i = sd_reduced, n1i = n_reduced,
  m2i = mean_control, sd2i = sd_control, n2i = n_control,
  data = soil
)

m <- rma(yi = yi, vi = vi, data = es, method = "REML")
summary(m)
predict(m, transf = exp)

forest(
  m,
  slab = paste(es$study_id, es$effect_id, sep = "."),
  atransf = exp,
  xlab = "Response ratio (reduced / conventional)"
)
abline(v = 1, lty = 2)

title: Solution 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Interpretation
A good answer separates the mean from variation. For example:

Across these synthetic studies, the model estimates the average proportional difference in soil carbon under reduced versus conventional tillage. The confidence interval describes uncertainty in that average effect. The prediction interval should be considered separately because it describes the range of underlying effects expected across comparable settings and may therefore be more relevant to local decisions.

Use the numerical values produced by your fitted model rather than copying this wording mechanically.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
section: A model output is not yet a conclusion
text:
A model output is not yet a conclusion




Interpretation reconnects the statistical model to the question we promised to answer.


Return explicitly to Module 0. A sophisticated model can still answer the wrong question. Ask participants what information, beyond the pooled estimate, they now think a conclusion needs.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
Module 8 — From model to conclusion
text:
Reconstruct the estimand
Before interpreting a number, complete the sentence:

Among [population/settings], what is the average effect of [intervention/exposure] compared with [comparator] on [outcome], measured as [effect measure], over [time frame]?


Does the evidence in the fitted model actually correspond to that estimand?


This catches estimand drift. Eligibility decisions, available outcomes and modelling choices may have shifted what was actually estimated relative to the review question.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
text:
Translate the effect scale
Suppose the pooled log response ratio is:
\[\hat\mu = 0.077\]
Then:
\[\exp(0.077) = 1.08\]
So the estimated average relative response is about 8% higher in the intervention group.

“8% higher” is not the same as “an 8 percentage-point increase”.


Use this to check scale literacy. Relative effects need a baseline to become absolute effects. Avoid language like “improved by 8%” unless the outcome and direction make “improved” defensible.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
text:
Relative effects need context
An 8% relative increase means different things from different baselines.
If the comparator mean were 20 units:
\[20 \times 1.08 = 21.6\]
If it were 100 units:
\[100 \times 1.08 = 108\]

Decision relevance often requires both relative and absolute interpretation.


Do not imply that the pooled ratio can always be safely applied to any baseline. This is an illustration of translation, and baseline risk/level may itself modify effects.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
section: Confidence interval and prediction interval answer different questions
text:
Confidence interval and prediction interval answer different questions
Confidence interval: uncertainty about the estimated mean effect.
Prediction interval: expected range of underlying effects in a comparable new setting, conditional on the model.

predict(m, transf = exp)


Could the mean be beneficial while effects in some settings are negligible or adverse?


Bring back Module 3. In heterogeneous agri-food systems this distinction can be central to management. A narrow CI around the mean does not imply consistent effects everywhere.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
section: Do not turn the result into a vote

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
section: Moderators can help — but do not overclaim
text:
Moderators can help — but do not overclaim
If effects appear larger after longer intervention durations, we can report an across-study association.
We usually cannot conclude from that alone:

increasing intervention duration will cause the effect to become larger.


Prediction from observed study characteristics is not automatically causal explanation.


Reconnect to Module 5. Confounding between study-level characteristics remains possible. Make the wording match the design and estimand.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
text:
Transportability is a separate question
A meta-analysis describes the studies included in the synthesis.
Applying it elsewhere requires asking:

Is the new population represented?
Are intervention implementation and comparator similar?
Are climate, soil, production system and follow-up comparable?
Are important effect modifiers distributed similarly?
Are we interpolating or extrapolating?


A pooled estimate does not automatically travel.


This is particularly important in agri-food systems where environmental and management contexts vary greatly. Avoid implying that a random-effects model itself solves external validity.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
text:
Bring credibility into the conclusion
Interpretation should reflect:


Internal validityCould study results be biased?


AvailabilityCould important evidence be missing?


RobustnessDo defensible analytical choices change the story?



Precision cannot compensate for systematic bias.


A very precise synthesis of biased studies is still biased. Do not collapse these dimensions into a single quality score unless a specific framework requires it and its assumptions are justified.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
section: A useful results paragraph has layers
text:
A useful results paragraph has layers

What was synthesised?
What was the average magnitude and uncertainty?
How much did effects vary?
What explained variation, if anything?
How credible and robust is the evidence?
Where does the conclusion apply?


This is the scaffold for the final exercise. Not every paper needs six sentences, but every conclusion should have considered these six questions.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
text:
Worked example

Across the included studies, reduced tillage was associated with an estimated average increase in soil carbon of approximately 8% relative to conventional tillage (95% CI: 3% to 13%). Effects varied appreciably among studies, and the prediction interval included little or no benefit in some comparable settings. Some variation was associated with intervention duration, although this across-study relationship should not be interpreted causally. Results were broadly similar across prespecified sensitivity analyses, but incomplete reporting in parts of the evidence base means the average effect should be interpreted cautiously.


Numbers here are a teaching example and should be replaced by the fitted teaching-data values if the dataset changes. Ask learners to identify which phrase corresponds to magnitude, uncertainty, heterogeneity, moderators, robustness and reporting bias.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
section: What would you tell a decision-maker?
text:
What would you tell a decision-maker?
Not:

“Reduced tillage increases soil carbon by 8%.”

A more useful answer is conditional:

“Across the settings represented in the evidence, soil carbon was higher on average under reduced tillage, but effects varied among contexts. The average effect is therefore useful as a summary, not a guarantee for every setting.”


What additional local information would you want before making a recommendation?


Let participants supply the context variables. This is where evidence synthesis meets decision-making rather than replacing it.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
text:
Final synthesis: the whole course


Question +estimand


→


Effect sizes +variance


→


Model +heterogeneity


→


Credibility +interpretation


Then ask throughout:

Are effects dependent?
What explains variation?
Are conclusions robust?
What evidence might be missing?
To which settings can the result reasonably apply?


This slide is the conceptual map of Modules 0–8. Meta-analysis is a chain of linked decisions, not a single statistical command.

title: Module 8 — From model to conclusion
text:
Take-home message

A good meta-analysis does not merely produce a pooled number. It makes explicit what was estimated, how uncertain and variable it is, how credible the evidence is, and where the conclusion can reasonably apply.


End by asking participants to return to the estimand they wrote in Module 0 and write one final evidence statement. Their conclusion should be recognisably connected to the original question.

title: Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
section: Start with the assumptions that could matter
text:
Start with the assumptions that could matter


EvidenceWhich studies/effects belong in the synthesis?


MeasurementHow were outcomes converted to a common effect?


ModelHow were heterogeneity and dependence represented?



Sensitivity analysis should target plausible sources of uncertainty.


Ask participants to list three decisions they made before fitting their own most recent meta-analysis. Those are candidates for sensitivity analysis if reasonable alternatives exist.

title: Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
section: Influence diagnostics answer a narrower question
text:
Influence diagnostics answer a narrower question

Is the fitted result unusually dependent on one study or effect?


m <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "REML")

leave1out(m)
influence(m)


An influential study is not automatically a bad study.


Influence is a property of the dataset/model combination. A large, precise or unusual study may legitimately be influential. Do not delete studies merely because a diagnostic flags them.

title: Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
section: Leave-one-out: what are we looking for?

title: Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
text:
Robustness is about the conclusion




Use this as the anchor. Some estimates move more than others. Ask participants whether the overall story is stable and what would need to be reported. The point is not to demand identical results.

title: Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
text:
Model-specification sensitivity
Examples:

m_reml <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "REML")
m_pm   <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "PM")

m_mv <- rma.mv(
  yi, vi,
  random = ~ 1 | study_id/effect_id,
  data = es,
  method = "REML"
)


Which alternatives are scientifically defensible for this evidence base?


Do not encourage a kitchen-sink multiverse for its own sake. Compare alternatives that represent genuine uncertainty in the analysis. The estimator example is useful pedagogically, but dependence and eligibility decisions may matter far more.

title: Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
text:
Sensitivity to dependence assumptions
If a sampling correlation is unknown, we might repeat the analysis across plausible values:

\(\rho = 0.2\)    0.5    0.8

Then ask whether estimates and uncertainty materially change.

Make the unobserved assumption visible.


This links directly to Module 4. Do not imply these three rho values are universally appropriate; the plausible range must come from the design and subject matter.

title: Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
section: Risk of bias belongs in robustness thinking

title: Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
text:
What if the conclusion changes?
That is information, not analytical failure.

Identify which assumption drives the change.
Explain why both analyses are defensible—or why one is preferred.
Report the range of plausible conclusions.
Avoid choosing the specification because it gives the desired answer.


Fragility is itself a result.


This is an important cultural point. Sensitivity analysis is valuable precisely when it reveals that the conclusion depends on uncertain assumptions.

title: Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
text:
A compact reporting structure

The primary model estimated X. Results were similar when A and B were varied, but excluding studies with C shifted the estimate to Y and increased uncertainty. Conclusions are therefore robust to A/B, but sensitive to assumptions about C.


This is a template, not wording to copy mechanically. It forces authors to state what changed and what did not, rather than dumping a supplementary table of alternative models.

title: Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness
text:
Take-home message


Identify consequentialassumptions


→


Specify defensiblealternatives


→


Compare estimates +uncertainty


→


Report what isstable or fragile



Sensitivity analysis asks how much our conclusion depends on choices we could reasonably have made differently.


Transition to Module 7: one major threat cannot be solved simply by refitting the observed evidence—studies and outcomes that are missing because of selective reporting.

title: Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
section: One paper does not always mean one effect

title: Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
text:
Six rows — three studies




The key point is unequal information. If Study A contributes three highly related outcomes and Study B contributes one, simply treating all four as independent lets A count roughly three times. It can also make standard errors too small because correlation is ignored.

title: Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
text:
Where does dependence come from?


Shared unitsSeveral outcomes measured on the same plots, farms or animals.


Shared comparatorSeveral interventions compared with the same control group.


Repeated measurementThe same outcome measured at several times or depths.



Which of these would you expect in your own evidence base?


Invite examples. Make clear that study ID is not a magic definition of dependence: dependence arises from shared information and design. The study is often a useful clustering unit, but analysts need to understand how the effects were generated.

title: Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
section: What goes wrong if we ignore it?

title: Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
text:
Three common responses


Choose one effectSimple, but may discard relevant evidence and requires a defensible rule.


Combine effectsUseful when effects genuinely answer the same question and covariance can be handled.


Model dependenceRetain multiple effects and represent their structure explicitly.



The choice should follow the estimand and data-generating structure.


This links back to Module 0. Selecting one effect is not automatically wrong. Sometimes it is exactly what the estimand requires. The bad practice is choosing outcomes opportunistically after seeing results.

title: Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
text:
A simple multilevel model
For effect \(j\) within study \(i\):
\[y_{ij}=\mu+u_i+v_{ij}+e_{ij}\]

\(\mu\): average effect
\(u_i\): between-study deviation
\(v_{ij}\): within-study heterogeneity among underlying effects
\(e_{ij}\): sampling error


Keep the notation intuitive. We are decomposing why observed effects differ. Sampling error is already represented by vi; random effects describe heterogeneity at additional levels.

title: Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
text:
Fit it with rma.mv()

m_mv <- rma.mv(
  yi, vi,
  random = ~ 1 | study_id/effect_id,
  data = es,
  method = "REML"
)

summary(m_mv)


The nesting tells the model that effects are grouped within studies.


Explain the formula as study/effect, not as mysterious metafor syntax. In a real dataset, effect_id must uniquely identify effects within study. Compare this with the earlier rma() model that treated rows as independent.

title: Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
text:
Read the variance components
A multilevel model may estimate variation:

between studies — contexts differ;
within studies — outcomes/comparisons differ within the same study;
sampling error — observed estimates are noisy.


Which source of variation is scientifically interesting in your review?


Do not make variance decomposition purely technical. A large within-study component may indicate outcome-specific effects or treatment contrasts. A large between-study component may point to contextual variation. Interpretation depends on what each row represents.

title: Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
section: But random effects do not create missing covariance
text:
But random effects do not create missing covariance
If two estimates share participants or a control group, their sampling errors may be correlated.
A multilevel random-effects structure and a sampling covariance matrix address related but different problems.

# Conceptual form when a sampling V matrix is available
m_v <- rma.mv(
  yi,
  V = V,
  random = ~ 1 | study_id/effect_id,
  data = es
)


This is an important sophistication. The simple exercise uses vi because we do not know the sampling correlations. Make explicit that adding a study random effect does not magically reconstruct correlations induced by a shared control or repeated measures. Later analyses may use known covariance formulas, plausible correlations, or robust variance methods.

title: Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
text:
A useful diagnostic before modelling

with(es, table(study_id))

table(table(es$study_id))

Ask:

How many studies contribute >1 effect?
Why do they contribute more?
Do prolific studies differ systematically?
Which effects share data?


This simple table is often surprisingly informative. Encourage participants to map the dependence structure during extraction rather than discovering it only when fitting the model.

title: Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
Module 4 — Dependence is not optional
text:
Take-home message


Map thedependence


→


Decide whatbelongs together


→


Model orcombine it


→


Test keyassumptions



Dependence is a feature of the evidence — not an inconvenience to delete.


Transition to Module 5: once the dependence structure is represented, we can ask whether prespecified study characteristics explain some of the remaining heterogeneity.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
From effects to synthesis


Effect sizes


→


Precision


→


Model


→


Mean + variation



Pooling is a model-based summary, not a vote.


Reconnect to Module 1. We now have effect estimates and sampling variances. The task is to synthesise them without losing sight of the scientific quantity the model is supposed to estimate.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Why not just average?



Study A \(n=200\) small sampling variance



Study B \(n=10\) large sampling variance



Should these contribute equally to our estimate of the mean effect?


The larger study is not necessarily better; it is more statistically precise. Bias, relevance and precision remain separate issues.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Two reasons observed effects differ


Sampling variationRepeat the same underlying study and estimates will still vary.


Between-study heterogeneityUnderlying effects may genuinely differ among soils, climates, crops or implementations.


Observed variationWhat we see contains both sources.



Use the field-trial analogy: repeat exactly the same trial many times and estimates vary because of sampling. Move it between climates and soils and the underlying effect may vary too.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Common-effect or random-effects?


Common-effect
One underlying effect for the included studies.
Observed differences arise from sampling error.

Random-effects
Underlying effects may differ.
Estimate their mean and between-study variation.


Random effects do not make scientifically incompatible studies compatible.


Avoid presenting random effects as the automatic answer to heterogeneity. If studies estimate fundamentally different quantities, adding tau-squared does not rescue the estimand.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
The model in two lines
\[y_i=\theta_i+e_i\]
\[\theta_i=\mu+u_i\]


\(e_i\) = sampling error

\(u_i\) = between-study deviation


We want \(\mu\), but we also care about the spread around it.


Keep notation light. The point is to separate within-study sampling error from variation among underlying study effects. Module 3 will unpack that spread.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Fit the model

library(metafor)

soil <- read.csv("../data/teaching/soil_carbon.csv")

es <- escalc(
  measure = "ROM",
  m1i = mean_reduced, sd1i = sd_reduced, n1i = n_reduced,
  m2i = mean_control, sd2i = sd_control, n2i = n_control,
  data = soil
)

m <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "REML")
summary(m)


Explain REML briefly as a commonly used estimator of between-study variance. There is no need to compare all tau-squared estimators in this introductory module.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Don’t read the output top-to-bottom
Start with four questions:

What is the estimated mean effect?
How uncertain is that mean?
How much do underlying effects vary?
What does this mean on the original, interpretable scale?


This is a deliberate antidote to reading every p-value printed by software. Participants should develop a hierarchy for interpretation.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Back-transform the mean

predict(m, transf = exp)

If the pooled \(RR=1.10\):

Soil organic carbon is estimated to be 10% higher on average under reduced tillage than conventional tillage in the evidence represented by the model.


The final phrase matters. “Reduced tillage increases soil carbon by 10%” is a stronger causal and general claim that may not be justified by the designs or target population.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
section: Forest plot: read the evidence, not just the diamond

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Anatomy of a forest plot




Read this from the studies outward, not from the diamond backward. Point estimates show magnitude and direction; horizontal lines show uncertainty; point size commonly reflects statistical precision; the diamond summarises the modelled mean. Crossing the null is not a label for whether an individual study ‘worked’.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Create the forest plot

forest(
  m,
  slab = paste(es$study_id, es$effect_id, sep = "."),
  atransf = exp,
  xlab = "Response ratio (reduced / conventional)"
)

abline(v = 1, lty = 2)



RR = 1
no proportional difference

RR > 1
higher under reduced tillage

RR < 1
lower under reduced tillage


atransf = exp displays results on the ratio scale while the analysis remains on lnRR. That gives interpretable labels without changing the fitted model.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
section: Confidence interval: uncertainty in the mean
text:
Confidence interval: uncertainty in the mean

How precisely have we estimated \(\mu\)?

A 95% confidence interval describes uncertainty around the estimated mean underlying effect.

It does not describe the likely effect in a new setting.


A precise mean can coexist with substantial variation among true effects. This is one of the most important distinctions in applied meta-analysis.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Prediction interval: variation across settings

What underlying effect might occur in a comparable new setting?

Conceptually:
\[\hat\mu \pm t\sqrt{SE(\hat\mu)^2+\hat\tau^2}\]

If the CI excludes no effect but the prediction interval spans benefit and harm, what should a decision-maker hear?


Say “comparable new setting” deliberately. Prediction intervals do not license extrapolation beyond the populations and contexts represented by the evidence.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
section: See the difference: CI versus PI
text:
See the difference: CI versus PI




Keep the centre fixed and point to the different widths. The confidence interval asks how well we know the mean. The prediction interval adds estimated between-study variation and asks about an underlying effect in a comparable setting. This distinction is often more useful than another significance test.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Same mean, very different message



Evidence base A Mean RR = 1.10 PI = 1.04–1.16
Effects are relatively consistent.



Evidence base B Mean RR = 1.10 PI = 0.82–1.48
Effects vary substantially.



The pooled mean alone cannot distinguish these stories.


These are illustrative numbers. Ask which evidence base is easier to use for a local decision and what extra information would be useful for B.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
section: Don’t vote count the forest plot

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
A better results sentence
Instead of:

“Most studies were significant, therefore reduced tillage works.”

Try:

“Across the included evidence, the estimated mean response was X%, with a 95% CI of … . Underlying effects varied, with a prediction interval of … .”


What would you add before making a management recommendation?


Likely additions: study design/risk of bias, applicability, contexts represented, uncertainty, possible effect modifiers, outcomes and trade-offs. This keeps statistical synthesis connected to evidence appraisal.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Practical 2 — Your first model
Open exercises/02-first-meta-analysis.qmd.


Fit


→


Plot


→


Predict


→


Explain


Final task: explain the result to a policy colleague without using “statistically significant” as the conclusion.

Allow 25–35 minutes. Encourage pairs to compare their final wording. The interpretation is at least as important as successfully running the code.

title: Module 2 — Your first meta-analysis
text:
Take-home

A pooled mean is one feature of a distribution of effects.

A useful synthesis communicates:
mean + uncertainty + variation + scope

Transition to Module 3: we have deliberately mentioned variation without examining it closely. Now we ask what heterogeneity actually means and how to communicate it.

This is an important distinction for people who have encountered meta-analysis as a statistics exercise. A sophisticated model cannot repair biased eligibility criteria, selective evidence, poor extraction, or incompatible outcomes.
Mention that critical appraisal should inform interpretation and, where appropriate, sensitivity analysis; it is not simply a box to tick.

title: Module 0 — From question to meta-analysis
section: Start with the decision or claim
text:
Start with the decision or claim
Suppose a policy colleague asks:

Does reduced tillage increase soil organic carbon?

Before opening R, ask:

Compared with what?
In which systems?
Over what time period?
Which measure of soil carbon?
What kind of effect would answer the question?


Give participants 60–90 seconds in pairs. Ask them to identify what is underspecified. The aim is to show that apparently simple questions hide multiple analytical choices.

title: Module 0 — From question to meta-analysis
text:
The question contains an estimand
An estimand is the quantity we want to estimate.
For our running example:

The average proportional difference in soil organic carbon under reduced tillage compared with conventional tillage, across eligible field studies and relevant agri-food contexts.

We still need to define:
Population/context · Intervention · Comparator · Outcome · Effect measure · Target quantity

Do not make this overly technical. “Estimand” is useful because it forces us to say exactly what number we want the synthesis to estimate.
Point out that the target quantity might be an average effect, a distribution of effects, an effect in a particular context, or something else. The pooled mean is not automatically the most decision-relevant target.

title: Module 0 — From question to meta-analysis
text:
A useful translation exercise
Broad question

Does reduced tillage improve soil carbon?

More explicit synthesis question

Among agricultural field systems, what is the proportional difference in soil organic carbon under reduced or no tillage versus conventional tillage at the end of follow-up?

Effect measure
\[\ln(RR)=\ln\left(\frac{\bar X_{reduced}}{\bar X_{control}}\right)\]

Explain why the response ratio is attractive here: soil carbon is positive, studies may use different absolute scales, and a proportional effect has a meaningful interpretation. This is not a universal rule; Module 1 deals with choosing effect measures.

section: The data do not define the question
text:
The data do not define the question
A common workflow is:

“These are the outcomes reported in the papers. Which can we meta-analyse?”

A stronger workflow is:

“This is the quantity our question requires. Which reported results estimate it?”

That distinction helps prevent estimand drift.

Give an example: the management question concerns long-term soil carbon, but most studies report short-term microbial activity. Those data may be interesting, but pooling them does not answer the original question.

title: Module 0 — From question to meta-analysis
text:
Before you meta-analyse: five questions

What quantity do I want to estimate?
Do the included effects estimate that quantity?
Are the effects comparable enough to synthesise?
Are observations statistically independent?
What sources of bias or uncertainty affect interpretation?


These questions can become a recurring checklist throughout the course. Question 4 foreshadows the multilevel module. Question 5 links the statistical training back to evidence-synthesis practice.

title: Module 0 — From question to meta-analysis
Module 0 — From question to meta-analysis
text:
Take-home message

The question determines the estimand.
The estimand determines which effects are compatible.
Only then should the model be chosen.

Next: How do we put compatible study results onto an appropriate effect-size scale?

Return to the opening question: what does meta-analysis give us? Ideally participants now answer in terms of estimating a defined quantity and its uncertainty/distribution, rather than merely “combining studies”.

title: Practical Meta-analysis for Evidence Synthesis in the Agri-food Sector
text:
This open teaching package introduces quantitative evidence synthesis using R and metafor, with examples framed around agri-food research.
The course follows a question-first workflow:
Question → estimand → compatible evidence → effect size → model → uncertainty → interpretation.
It is designed for instructor-led workshops and self-directed learning.

Explain why a study-level random effect does not necessarily solve correlation caused by shared controls or repeated measurements.

This course treats meta-analysis as part of evidence synthesis, not simply as a statistical procedure. The recurring sequence is:

Question → estimand → compatible evidence → effect size → model → heterogeneity → dependence → moderators → robustness → interpretation

Modules 0–3 form the introductory core and can be taught as a half-day intensive session or expanded with exercises into a full day.

Presenter notes
Every RevealJS deck contains ::: {.notes} blocks. These are intended as teaching prompts rather than a script that must be read verbatim. They identify discussion questions, common misconceptions and transitions.

text:
Teaching dataset
data/teaching/soil_carbon.csv is synthetic. It is deliberately simple and should not be presented as empirical evidence about reduced tillage. The final EU-NESA package can supplement it with openly licensed empirical agri-food datasets where permissions and provenance are clear.

title: Instructor guide
text:
R setup
Participants need:
install.packages(c("metafor", "tidyverse"))
The introductory exercises primarily use metafor; dplyr is used for readable data manipulation.

title: Instructor guide
text:
Key messages to protect

The effect measure follows from the estimand.
Precision is not the same as methodological quality.
Random effects do not make conceptually incompatible studies compatible.
Do not interpret individual statistical significance by vote counting.
\(I^2\) is not a quality score or a universal traffic-light measure.
Prediction intervals can be more decision-relevant than the confidence interval around the mean.
Causal interpretation depends on study design and assumptions, not on meta-analysis alone.

title: Instructor guide
text:
Modules 4–6: suggested teaching plan

Module 4 — Dependence is not optional (35–45 min + 30 min practical)
Use participants’ own examples of multiple outcomes, time points and shared controls before introducing rma.mv(). The conceptual goal is to recognise dependence and map its source; the software is secondary. Explicitly distinguish random-effects clustering from sampling covariance.


Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity (35–45 min + 30 min practical)
Ask learners to state a biological moderator hypothesis before fitting a model. Keep the causal warning prominent: most meta-regressions compare study characteristics across studies, even when treatment allocation within the primary studies was randomised. Focus reporting on estimates, uncertainty, data support and residual heterogeneity rather than moderator p-values.


Module 6 — Sensitivity and robustness (30–40 min + 30 min practical)
Begin by asking which analytical choices in the synthesis were genuinely uncertain. Separate influence diagnostics from sensitivity analyses. The endpoint is a robustness statement describing which conclusions are stable to which tested assumptions; avoid reducing robustness to whether statistical significance changes.

title: Instructor guide
section: Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
text:
Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
Suggested time: 40–50 minutes teaching + 25–35 minutes practical.
The central teaching principle is that funnel plots and regression tests identify patterns, not the mechanism that caused them. Start with the reporting process, then introduce statistical diagnostics. Encourage triangulation across search/extraction information, study characteristics and statistical patterns. Avoid teaching trim-and-fill as a correction procedure.

title: Instructor guide
text:
Module 8 — From model to conclusion
Suggested time: 40–50 minutes teaching + 30 minutes synthesis exercise.
Use this as the capstone. Participants should return to the estimand from Module 0 and build a conclusion from magnitude, uncertainty, variation, credibility and applicability. The final exercise works well in pairs: one participant writes the technical paragraph and the other rewrites it for a decision-maker, then they compare what information was lost.

title: Recommended reading
Module 1 — Effect sizes
section: The job of an effect size
text:
The job of an effect size


Study result


→


Comparable effect


→


Sampling variance


→


Meta-analysis



The effect measure defines what we are synthesising.


Open with the conceptual job rather than a formula. Meta-analysis needs study results expressed on a scale that has a consistent meaning across studies, plus an estimate of their sampling uncertainty. Emphasise that choosing an effect size is part of defining the estimand; it is not merely data preparation.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
Module 1 — Effect sizes
text:
One comparison, several possible effects




Reduced tillage

Ask: which is easiest to interpret? Then: which would still make sense if another study used a different unit or had a very different baseline? The same raw data can answer subtly different questions depending on the effect measure.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
section: Mean difference: keep the original unit
text:
Mean difference: keep the original unit
\[MD = \bar X_T - \bar X_C\]


Useful when

the outcome is measured on the same scale;
the unit itself is meaningful;
an absolute change answers the question.



Interpretation “Yield was 0.6 t/ha higher.”
Null = 0



The original unit is often a major advantage. Do not standardise simply because meta-analysis software makes it easy. If tonnes per hectare is the decision-relevant quantity, preserve it.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
section: Standardised mean difference: change the question
text:
Standardised mean difference: change the question
\[SMD = \frac{\bar X_T-\bar X_C}{SD_{pooled}}\]

The effect is now expressed in standard deviation units. Is that the quantity your users need?


Useful for a similar construct measured on genuinely different scales.
Often reported as Hedges’ g after small-sample correction.
Differences in SD can reflect populations and measurement, not just scale.


This is an important warning slide. SMD is not a generic solution to different units. Standardisation changes the estimand. Mention Hedges’ g, but keep the focus on interpretation rather than formulae.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
text:
Response ratio: proportional change
\[RR=\frac{\bar X_T}{\bar X_C}\]
We usually analyse:
\[\ln(RR)=\ln(\bar X_T)-\ln(\bar X_C)\]


Ratio scale
Null = 1

Log scale
Null = 0


Explain why the log scale is useful: proportional increases and decreases become more symmetric. A doubling and halving are +0.693 and −0.693. The model can live on the log scale while interpretation returns to the ratio scale.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
text:
Back-transform before you communicate

\(\ln(RR)=0.095\)
↓
\(RR=e^{0.095}\approx1.10\)
↓
about 10% higher

\[\%\Delta = 100\times(RR-1)\]

For negative effects, avoid casual symmetry claims on the percentage scale. RR = 0.80 means 20% lower. Encourage participants to back-transform before explaining results to non-technical audiences.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
section: Choose the measure from the question
text:
Choose the measure from the question


AbsoluteHow many t/ha more yield?→ Mean difference


StandardisedHow large is the difference relative to within-study variability?→ SMD


ProportionalWhat proportional change in SOC occurs?→ Response ratio



Meaning first. Convenience second.


Ask participants for examples from their own work. This is illustrative, not a mechanical decision rule. Study design, outcome distribution and data structure also matter.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
text:
Three measures, three meanings




Use this as the synthesis slide before the decision exercise. The choice is not about which statistic is most sophisticated; it is about which quantity answers the review question while remaining comparable across studies.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
text:
A 60-second decision exercise
Which effect measure would you start with?

Fertiliser increases wheat yield, reported as kg/ha in every study.
Animal welfare is measured using several validated continuous scales.
Soil carbon is reported in several units, but the question is proportional change relative to control.


What scientific interpretation would each choice imply?


Suggested starting answers: MD; possibly SMD if the scales genuinely measure the same construct; response ratio. Stress that the justification matters more than the label.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
section: Effect size alone is not enough
text:
Effect size alone is not enough
Two studies can estimate the same effect but with very different precision.
For independent groups, an approximate variance for \(\ln(RR)\) is:
\[v_i=\frac{SD_T^2}{n_T\bar X_T^2}+\frac{SD_C^2}{n_C\bar X_C^2}\]

Effect estimate + sampling variance travel together.


Do not derive the equation. The conceptual point is that an estimate from a small noisy experiment carries less information than the same estimate from a precise experiment.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
Module 1 — Effect sizes
text:
Calculate lnRR with metafor

library(metafor)

soil <- read.csv("../data/teaching/soil_carbon.csv")

es <- escalc(
  measure = "ROM",
  m1i = mean_reduced, sd1i = sd_reduced, n1i = n_reduced,
  m2i = mean_control, sd2i = sd_control, n2i = n_control,
  data = soil
)

ROM = log response ratio of means.

Group 1 is reduced tillage and group 2 conventional. Direction matters. Ask participants to write the intended contrast in words before running the code: reduced divided by conventional.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
text:
Inspect before modelling

es |>
  transform(
    RR = exp(yi),
    percent_change = 100 * (RR - 1)
  ) |>
  subset(select = c(study_id, yi, vi, RR, percent_change))


Are signs and directions sensible?
Any impossible values or extreme variances?
Duplicated effects?
Does the effect measure still answer the question?


Calculation is not validation. Encourage participants to inspect several rows and manually reproduce at least one effect whenever establishing a new workflow.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
text:
Manual check: Study A

\(\ln(RR)=\ln(22.1/20.0)\approx0.100\)
\(RR\approx1.105\)
SOC ≈ 10.5% higher under reduced tillage


Opposite sign? First check the treatment/comparator direction.


Direction errors are easy to make and can propagate through an entire synthesis. This simple manual check is one of the cheapest quality-control steps available.

title: Module 1 — Effect sizes
text:
Common traps

Mixing endpoint values and change scores without considering the estimand.
Treating different outcome definitions as interchangeable.
Reversing treatment and comparator.
Using SMD simply because studies report different units.
Ignoring shared controls or repeated measurements.
Transforming effects without propagating uncertainty.


The shared-control point foreshadows Module 4 on dependence. Calculating multiple effects from one experiment does not make them independent observations.

Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
section: The average can hide the decision problem
text:
The average can hide the decision problem

+30%   +25%   +20%   +5%   0%   −10%


The average is positive. Is “the intervention increases the outcome” an adequate summary?


Give participants a moment. A farmer or policymaker may care more about where the intervention works, whether it can fail, and whether their context resembles the evidence base. This is the scientific motivation for heterogeneity.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
section: In agri-food research, variation is expected
text:
In agri-food research, variation is expected


Environmentclimate · soil · baseline condition


Managementintensity · duration · implementation


Systemcrop · livestock · landscape context



Context dependence may be the scientific result.


Avoid presenting heterogeneity as a nuisance or failure. For many management interventions, understanding context dependence is precisely what users need from the synthesis.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
Three quantities — three different questions


\(\tau^2\)How much between-study variance is estimated?Squared effect-size units


\(\tau\)What is the SD of underlying effects?Same scale as the analysed effect


\(I^2\)How large is heterogeneity relative to observed sampling variation?A relative percentage



This slide is the map. The next slides unpack each quantity. Stress that none is a universal measure of “how bad” the meta-analysis is.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
\(\tau^2\): between-study variance
\[\theta_i \sim N(\mu,\tau^2)\]
\(\tau^2\) is the estimated variance among underlying study effects.

Useful for modelling — but are squared effect-size units easy to interpret?


Tau-squared is the parameter commonly printed by software and used in random-effects weights. Its squared units make direct substantive interpretation awkward.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
section: \(\tau\): put spread back on the effect-size scale
text:
\(\tau\): put spread back on the effect-size scale
\[\tau=\sqrt{\tau^2}\]
For lnRR, \(\tau\) is the SD of underlying effects on the log-ratio scale.

There is no universal “small / medium / large” threshold for \(\tau\).


The substantive importance of tau depends on the effect scale and the decision context. A particular amount of variation may be trivial for one outcome and decisive for another.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
\(I^2\): relative, not absolute
A common description is the proportion of observed variation attributable to heterogeneity rather than sampling variation.
But \(I^2\) depends on:

between-study heterogeneity; and
the precision of the included studies.


The same \(\tau^2\) can coexist with different \(I^2\) values.


This is why I-squared is not a direct measure of biological variability. More precise studies can yield a high I-squared even when absolute between-study variation is modest.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
\(I^2\) is not a traffic light

Be cautious: 25% = low · 50% = moderate · 75% = high

Those labels do not tell us whether variation is scientifically important.

Could the plausible range of effects change the decision?


Do not tell participants never to report I-squared. It can be useful descriptive information. The problem is converting generic thresholds into substantive conclusions.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
Prediction intervals make variation tangible
Suppose:

Mean RR = 1.10
95% prediction interval = 0.82–1.48


A comparable setting could plausibly show a decrease or a substantial increase. Is the mean enough?


These values are illustrative rather than outputs from the teaching dataset. Ask which interval—CI or PI—is more relevant to someone deciding whether to implement the intervention locally.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
Confidence interval ≠ prediction interval


Confidence interval
How uncertain is our estimate of the mean effect?

Prediction interval
What underlying effect might occur in a comparable new setting?


Different questions → different intervals.


A narrow confidence interval does not imply effects are consistent. The mean can be precisely estimated while true effects vary widely.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
Inspect heterogeneity in metafor

m <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "REML")

m$tau2
sqrt(m$tau2)
m$I2

predict(m, transf = exp)


Don’t copy these numbers into a paper. Interpret them together.


For lnRR, back-transform pooled and predicted effects to response ratios before explaining them. Keep the distinction between the modelling scale and the communication scale clear.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
section: Ask “why might effects differ?” before testing moderators
text:
Ask “why might effects differ?” before testing moderators


Biologyrainfall · soil texture · crop · baseline carbon


Implementationduration · intensity · co-interventions


Methodsmeasurement · design · analysis · risk of bias



Ask participants to nominate plausible effect modifiers before inspecting associations. This encourages hypothesis-led analysis rather than searching through variables after seeing the data.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
section: Not all heterogeneity is ecological signal

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
section: Should we explain every bit of heterogeneity?

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
section: Same mean does not mean same evidence
text:
Same mean does not mean same evidence




If you report only the pooled mean, these evidence bases look the same.


This is the visual anchor for the module. Both panels have the same vertical mean line. In A, effects cluster around it. In B, the mean hides substantial context dependence. Ask which panel makes the pooled mean more portable to a new setting and why.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
Same mean, different decisions



Scenario A Mean benefit ≈ 10% Effects tightly clustered around benefit



Scenario B Mean benefit ≈ 10% Effects range from meaningful harm to large benefit



What information would you seek before applying Scenario B locally?


Expected answers include context, moderators, study design, applicability, baseline conditions and uncertainty. The point is to connect heterogeneity to decisions rather than to a diagnostic threshold.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
Practical 3 — Tell the scientific story
Open exercises/03-heterogeneity.qmd.
You will compare meta-analyses with similar means but different heterogeneity, then inspect the soil-carbon example.

Final task: write four sentences for a decision-maker without using “low”, “moderate” or “high” heterogeneity.


If time is short, prioritise the final interpretation task over extra calculations. Ask pairs to read their four sentences aloud and compare what information they chose to foreground.

title: Module 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
Take-home

Heterogeneity is not a nuisance statistic attached to the pooled effect.

A useful synthesis communicates:

centre + uncertainty + variation + context


End by returning to the question from Module 0. Would a single average effect answer it? What additional information would participants now want before using the synthesis for a decision?

title: Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
text:
Heterogeneity invites a better question
Instead of:

“Is heterogeneity significant?”

ask:

Which scientifically plausible characteristics might explain why effects differ?


Module 3 established that heterogeneity may be substantive information. Here we move from describing variation to asking whether measured study characteristics are associated with it.

title: Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
section: Start with a hypothesis, not a variable list

title: Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
text:
Categorical moderators: subgroup differences

m_climate <- rma.mv(
  yi, vi,
  mods = ~ climate,
  random = ~ 1 | study_id/effect_id,
  data = es
)

summary(m_climate)

The intercept represents the reference category; other coefficients represent differences from it.

Make learners inspect factor coding with levels(es$climate). The coefficient is a difference on the log response-ratio scale, not a separate pooled effect unless transformed appropriately.

title: Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
text:
Continuous moderators: a slope

m_duration <- rma.mv(
  yi, vi,
  mods = ~ duration,
  random = ~ 1 | study_id/effect_id,
  data = es
)

\[y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{duration}_i+u_i+e_i\]

What does a one-year increase in duration mean on the lnRR scale?


Beta1 is the expected change in lnRR per one-unit increase in duration. exp(beta1) is the multiplicative change in RR per year. Emphasise units. Rescaling duration to five years can sometimes make interpretation easier.

title: Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
text:
Back-transform the slope carefully
Suppose \(\beta_1=0.025\) per year.
\[\exp(0.025)=1.025\]
That corresponds to approximately a 2.5% multiplicative increase in RR per additional year, conditional on the model.

It does not mean that extending the same experiment by one year would necessarily cause a 2.5% larger effect.


This distinction is crucial. The meta-regression compares studies with different durations. Longer-duration studies may differ in many other ways.

title: Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
section: Meta-regression is usually observational across studies
text:
Meta-regression is usually observational across studies




Even if treatments were randomised within every primary study, duration, climate or study design generally were not randomised across studies. Meta-regression therefore does not inherit the causal protection of the treatment randomisation.

title: Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
section: How many moderators can the data support?
text:
How many moderators can the data support?
Meta-regression is often information-poor.

A meta-analysis with 12 studies does not become a rich regression dataset because it has 30 dependent effect sizes.
Sparse categories yield unstable estimates.
Multiple testing increases opportunities for chance findings.
Moderator measurement error can attenuate associations.


Avoid mechanical “10 studies per moderator” rules — but be appropriately modest with small evidence bases.


There is no universal magic ratio. Precision depends on distributions, heterogeneity, dependence and effect sizes. The practical lesson is restraint, prespecification and honest uncertainty.

title: Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
section: Multivariable models need a causal story too
text:
Multivariable models need a causal story too

m_both <- rma.mv(
  yi, vi,
  mods = ~ duration + climate,
  random = ~ 1 | study_id/effect_id,
  data = es
)

Adding covariates can change the estimand of each coefficient.

Are we adjusting for a confounder, a proxy, a mediator, or merely an available variable?


This is a light introduction to causal thinking, not a full DAG lesson. Encourage reviewers to articulate why each variable is included. “It reduced tau-squared” is not sufficient justification.

title: Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
section: Residual heterogeneity is not model failure
text:
Residual heterogeneity is not model failure
After adding moderators, ask:

Is there evidence of an association?
How uncertain is it?
How much heterogeneity remains?
Are predictions still variable across settings?
Does the moderator cover the range where we want to predict?


The goal is understanding, not making \(\tau^2\) disappear.


Do not select a model simply because it explains the largest fraction of heterogeneity. A flexible model can overfit a small meta-analysis.

title: Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
text:
Extrapolation deserves a warning label
If durations in the evidence base range from 2–12 years:

Predict at 8 years? ✓     Predict at 30 years? ?


A fitted line is mathematically happy to extrapolate where the evidence does not exist.


This is particularly important for decision support. Show the observed moderator range alongside predictions. A linear trend may also be biologically implausible over long horizons.

title: Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
section: Report the pattern, not just the p-value

title: Module 5 — Explaining heterogeneity
text:
Take-home message


Hypothesis


→


Moderatormodel


→


Association +uncertainty


→


Cautiousinterpretation



Meta-regression can describe context dependence. It does not automatically explain its cause.


Transition to Module 6: every synthesis contains analytical choices. We now ask whether the substantive conclusion is robust to reasonable alternatives and influential evidence.

title: Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
section: The meta-analysis only sees available evidence
text:
The meta-analysis only sees available evidence




Missingness can occur at the study, outcome, analysis and result level.


Begin with the mechanism rather than a funnel plot. Ask: what has to happen between collecting data and a result appearing in our review? Distinguish non-publication of whole studies from selective reporting within studies. In agri-food research, grey literature, reports and multiple outcomes can make availability especially complicated.

title: Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
section: Publication bias is only one mechanism
text:
Publication bias is only one mechanism


Study publicationWhether an entire study becomes available.


Outcome reportingWhich measured outcomes appear in the report.


Analysis reportingWhich time points, contrasts or models are shown.



Could availability depend on the direction, magnitude or statistical significance of the result?


Use “reporting bias” as the umbrella idea. A published paper does not guarantee that every measured outcome or analysis is available. Ask participants for examples: yield reported but soil carbon omitted; only one follow-up time; subgroup reported after seeing results.

title: Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
section: Funnel plots: what are they showing?
text:
Funnel plots: what are they showing?




A funnel plot visualises the relationship between effect estimates and their precision. In the absence of several complications, estimates from smaller studies are expected to scatter more widely. Do not teach symmetry as a formal null expectation that diagnoses publication bias.

title: Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
crumbs: Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias

title: Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
text:
A funnel plot in metafor

m <- rma(yi, vi, data = es, method = "REML")
funnel(m)

Before interpreting the picture, ask:

Are there enough independent studies for the pattern to be informative?
Could heterogeneity explain structure in the plot?
Are effect size and precision mathematically related?
Do study characteristics differ with study size?


Do not offer a universal minimum k as a magic threshold. The point is that sparse plots are difficult to interpret and dependence further complicates them.

title: Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
section: Small-study effects are not synonymous with publication bias
text:
Small-study effects are not synonymous with publication bias
A regression-based test asks whether effect size is associated with precision or sampling variance.

regtest(m)


A detected small-study effect does not identify its cause.


Explain that “Egger test = publication bias test” is an overstatement. The regression can detect a pattern consistent with small-study effects; selection is one possible explanation. Conversely, low power means a non-significant test cannot establish absence of bias.

title: Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
section: What does a non-significant test tell us?
text:
What does a non-significant test tell us?
Not this:

“There was no publication bias (p > 0.05).”

Better:

“We found no clear evidence of a relationship between effect size and precision, but the analysis has limited ability to rule out selective reporting.”


Ask the group what evidence would be required to support the first sentence. This links back to the course-wide theme that absence of statistical significance is not evidence of absence.
crumbs: Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias

title: Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
text:
What about trim-and-fill?
Trim-and-fill can be useful as an exploratory sensitivity analysis, but it relies on assumptions about funnel asymmetry that may not match the actual selection process.

m_tf <- trimfill(m)
funnel(m_tf)


Do not describe the filled estimate as the result “corrected for publication bias”.


The method imputes hypothetical missing effects under a particular symmetry model. It does not recover unknown unpublished studies and does not establish why asymmetry occurred.

Triangulate, do not tick a box
A useful assessment combines:


Review-process evidenceWhat appears to be missing?


Study characteristicsCould size and design explain patterns?


Statistical patternsAre small-study effects apparent?



The conclusion is an argument from multiple pieces of evidence.


Avoid converting this into a score. The goal is transparent reasoning about mechanisms and consequences.

title: Module 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
text:
Reporting example

Smaller studies tended to report larger effects, although study size was also associated with intervention duration and setting. Funnel-plot asymmetry and regression diagnostics therefore cannot be attributed uniquely to selective publication. Searches identified several reports with incomplete outcome information. We consider selective reporting a plausible source of bias and interpret the pooled estimate cautiously.


Point out the structure: observed pattern → competing explanation → direct review evidence → calibrated conclusion. It does not pretend the cause has been proven.

title: Solution 1 — Effect sizes
text:
library(metafor)
library(dplyr)

soil <- read.csv("../data/teaching/soil_carbon.csv")

es <- escalc(
  measure = "ROM",
  m1i = mean_reduced, sd1i = sd_reduced, n1i = n_reduced,
  m2i = mean_control, sd2i = sd_control, n2i = n_control,
  data = soil
) |>
  mutate(
    RR = exp(yi),
    percent_change = 100 * (RR - 1)
  )

For Study A, \(\ln(22.1/20.0)\approx0.100\), giving \(RR\approx1.105\): the treatment mean is about 10.5% higher than the comparator mean.

title: Solution 1 — Effect sizes
text:
Effect-measure discussion

Mean difference is directly interpretable if tonnes/ha is common and meaningful across studies.
SMD/Hedges’ g may be defensible if the scales genuinely measure the same construct, although the change in estimand and interpretability should be considered.
Response ratio / log response ratio matches a proportional soil-carbon question when means are positive.

The key is not that these are universal rules: the effect measure should correspond to the target estimand and available design/data.

title: Solution 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
Part B

m$tau2          # estimated between-study variance
sqrt(m$tau2)    # between-study SD, on the lnRR scale
m$I2            # relative heterogeneity statistic
predict(m, transf = exp)  # mean and prediction interval on RR scale

Interpret these quantities together. \(I^2\) should not be converted mechanically into a qualitative traffic-light label.

title: Solution 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
Part C
Plausible hypotheses include intervention duration, climate, soil properties, crop system, baseline carbon and management intensity. The teaching dataset contains duration and climate, but not all of these candidate moderators. Absence of a measured moderator does not mean it is unimportant.

title: Solution 3 — Understanding heterogeneity
text:
Part D
A strong answer communicates the estimated mean and its confidence interval, then explicitly distinguishes that uncertainty from between-study variation and the prediction interval. It should restrict inference to settings reasonably represented by the included evidence.

title: Solution 5 — Meta-regression and effect modification
text:
2. Continuous moderator

m_duration <- rma.mv(
  yi, vi,
  mods = ~ duration,
  random = ~ 1 | study_id/effect_id,
  data = es
)
summary(m_duration)

exp(coef(m_duration)["duration"])

The duration coefficient is the expected difference in lnRR associated with a one-year difference in study duration. Exponentiating it gives the multiplicative change in RR associated with one additional year across the studies represented by the model. Inspect the confidence interval before deciding whether the data estimate that pattern precisely.

title: Solution 5 — Meta-regression and effect modification
text:
3. Categorical moderator

es$climate <- factor(es$climate)
levels(es$climate)

m_climate <- rma.mv(
  yi, vi,
  mods = ~ climate,
  random = ~ 1 | study_id/effect_id,
  data = es
)
summary(m_climate)

The intercept corresponds to the factor’s reference climate. Each displayed climate coefficient is a contrast with that reference on the lnRR scale. It is not, by itself, the pooled effect for that climate category.

title: Solution 5 — Meta-regression and effect modification
text:
4. Two moderators

m_both <- rma.mv(
  yi, vi,
  mods = ~ duration + climate,
  random = ~ 1 | study_id/effect_id,
  data = es
)

The duration coefficient can change because duration and climate are associated in the evidence base. In the multivariable model it represents the duration association conditional on the included climate terms. With a small dataset, all such estimates should be treated cautiously.

title: Solution 5 — Meta-regression and effect modification
text:
5. Causal interpretation
A defensible rewrite is: “Across the included studies, longer-duration studies tended to show [larger/smaller] estimated effects, although this association is uncertain and may reflect other differences among studies.”
Potential confounders include climate, crop type, baseline soil carbon, soil texture, management intensity, study design or measurement method. Only some are measured in the teaching dataset.

title: Solution 5 — Meta-regression and effect modification
text:
6. Extrapolation
No strong prediction at 30 years is supported by data observed only over a much shorter range. The model will calculate a value, but this requires extrapolating the fitted functional form beyond represented evidence and may be biologically implausible.

title: Solution 5 — Meta-regression and effect modification
text:
7. Reporting
A strong paragraph reports the estimated association and interval, states the observed moderator range, notes remaining heterogeneity and explicitly describes the analysis as an across-study association rather than evidence that manipulating the moderator would cause the estimated change.

title: Solution 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
text:
2–3. Funnel plot and regression
The plot should first be described in terms of any relationship between effect estimates and precision. regtest() evaluates evidence of a small-study-effect pattern; it does not identify the mechanism producing that pattern. Genuine heterogeneity correlated with study size, design differences and chance are among alternative explanations. Limited information can also make the test insensitive, so a non-significant result does not establish absence of selective reporting.

title: Solution 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
text:
4. Trim-and-fill
A suitable statement is:

Trim-and-fill shows how the pooled estimate changes under a particular model of funnel-plot asymmetry; it does not identify or recover the actual missing studies and therefore should not be interpreted as a corrected estimate.

title: Solution 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
text:
5. Triangulation
A strong answer notes that the registration and incomplete abstracts provide direct reasons to suspect unavailable results, while the different production systems provide a competing explanation for small-study effects. The appropriate conclusion is therefore calibrated: selective reporting is plausible, but funnel asymmetry alone cannot identify its cause or magnitude.

title: Solution 7 — Missing evidence and reporting bias
text:
6. Reporting
For example:

We found no clear statistical evidence of an association between effect size and precision in the regression-based small-study-effect analysis. However, this does not rule out selective publication or outcome reporting, particularly given the limited information available to diagnose these processes.
